title: Mā no mahāntam: spare our great and our small
theme: Rudra is asked not to strike any of the household: the elder and the infant, the young man and the child unborn, father and mother, and the bodies the speakers hold dear.

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «गुरुप्रभृतिपूज्यवर्गं» — the elders, teachers and others to be honoured

words.meaning: the one who sprinkles (seed): the young man

words.gram: past pass. part. m. acc. sg.
words.meaning: the one sprinkled in: the child in the womb
words.context: The anonymous commentator: «योनिष्वासिक्तं गर्भस्थं पिण्डं» — the embryo, poured into the womb

words.role: main verb of the first line and a half

words.gram: f. acc. pl. (Vedic tanuvaḥ for tanvaḥ)

words.context: The anonymous commentator: «दुष्टरोदनकर्तः» — who makes the wicked weep

words.gram: verb, reduplicated aorist injunctive 2nd sg. active
words.role: main verb of the last clause

sandhi.type: visarga after a before a voiced consonant; final m before a vowel
sandhi.rule: naḥ before m becomes no; mahāntam is joined to uta.

sandhi.type: visarga after a before a vowel other than a
sandhi.rule: naḥ before u drops its visarga and stands in hiatus: na ukṣantam.

sandhi.type: visarga after a before a; the a kept
sandhi.rule: naḥ before a becomes no, and here the following a is kept, not elided (no arbhakam, not no ’rbhakam): see sandhi exceptions.
ā + u becomes o: mā uta → mota.

sandhi.type: visarga after ā before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: āḥ before a voiced sound drops its visarga: priyāḥ mā → priyā mā.

sandhi.type: visarga before t; visarga after a before a voiced consonant
sandhi.rule: naḥ before t becomes nas; tanuvaḥ before r becomes tanuvo.

sandhi_exceptions.note: naḥ arbhakam is written no arbhakam: the visarga becomes o, but the initial a of arbhakam is kept, as in the Ṛgveda’s text of this verse, where classical sandhi would elide it (no ’rbhakam).

morphology.note: The one verb governs the whole first line and the first half of the second: ‘do not strike our great one … nor our mother’. After mā the aorist has no augment, P. 6.4.74 (न माङ्योगे).
Accusative plural of tanū written with the Vedic -uv- (tanuvaḥ) where classical Sanskrit writes tanvaḥ.
Present participle of √ukṣ, ‘sprinkle’; the commentator glosses it as the young man able to beget. Its pair ukṣitam, the past participle, is ‘what has been sprinkled in’, the child in the womb.

translation.literal: Do not [strike] our great one, nor our small one; do not [strike] our sprinkling one, nor our sprinkled one; do not strike our father, nor [our] mother; do not harm our dear bodies, O Rudra.
translation.readable: Do not strike the old among us or the very young, the man in his strength or the child not yet born; do not strike our father or our mother; Rudra, do not harm the lives we hold dear.

anvaya: हे रुद्र नः महान्तम् मा [वधीः] उत नः अर्भकम् मा [वधीः] नः उक्षन्तम् मा उत नः उक्षितम् मा नः पितरम् मा वधीः मा उत मातरम् नः प्रियाः तनुवः मा रीरिषः ।
syntax: A list of objects, each with mā and the enclitic naḥ, all depending on the one verb vadhīḥ, which comes only in the second line; a last clause has its own verb rīriṣaḥ with the vocative rudra. The pairs are built on contrast: great and small, the one who begets and the one begotten, father and mother.

ambiguities.note: The two participles of √ukṣ are read by the commentator as the young man and the embryo. The words themselves say only ‘the sprinkling’ and ‘the sprinkled’; the pairing with great and small supports a sequence of the generations.

metre.name: jagatī
metre.note: Two lines of 24 syllables (12 + 12 each), a regular jagatī as printed.

beginner: This prayer is addressed to Rudra, a god feared for his power to strike and prayed to for protection. It asks him not to strike anyone in the family, and it names them in pairs: the old and the very young, the man in his strength and the child still in the womb, the father and the mother. It ends by asking him not to harm "the bodies we hold dear". The same verse is found in the Ṛgveda and in the Śrī Rudram, the great hymn to Rudra in the Yajurveda, with small differences of wording. In the Mahānārāyaṇa it stands among short prayers for protection that come before the offering formulas. The old commentator explains each word: the great are elders and teachers, the small one is a nursing infant. The edition reports this; it makes no claim about what reciting it does.
analogy: Like a roll call of a whole household read out at the door: every generation is named so that none is left out.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: It asks Rudra not to strike the great one and the small one, the sprinkling one and the sprinkled one, the father and the mother, and not to harm the dear bodies of the speakers.

commentary.q: How does the commentator explain the pairs?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: The anonymous commentator explains Rudra as the one who makes the wicked weep, «हे रुद्र दुष्टरोदनकर्तः». The great one is the class of elders and teachers to be honoured, «गुरुप्रभृतिपूज्यवर्गं»; the small one is the suckling, «स्तनंधयम्»; the sprinkled one is the embryo, «योनिष्वासिक्तं गर्भस्थं पिण्डं». He gives the sense of the whole: «सर्वानस्मानस्मदीयांश्च सुखयेति भावः» — make all of us and ours happy.

commentary.q: How does it differ from the Ṛgveda?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: The Ṛgveda has the verse at 1.114.7, with the first line as here. Its last clause reads «मा नः प्रियास्तन्वो रुद्र रीरिषः», with the enclitic before priyāḥ and the classical tanvaḥ; the Mahānārāyaṇa has «प्रिया मा नस्तनुवो रुद्र रीरिषः», with the Vedic tanuvaḥ. The words are the same; their order and one spelling differ.

schools.disagreement: No Vedānta-school commentary on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources (Raṅgarāmānuja’s commentary on the Mahānārāyaṇa is not among them). The anonymous bhāṣya explains the words and the rite; it does not argue an Advaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita or Dvaita position here, so the edition gives none.

parallels.quote: मा नो महान्तमुत मा नो अर्भकं
parallels.note: The same verse in the Ṛgveda, in a hymn to Rudra; the second half orders its words differently (see commentary).

contemporary.text: The prayer asks nothing for the speaker alone; it names the whole household across the generations. Concern widened to the oldest and the not yet born is a measure of what a person counts as their own. This is a modern reflection on the passage, not part of its traditional meaning.

reflect.beginner: Who would you name, in pairs, if you made such a list for your own family?
reflect.deeper: Why might the verse be built on pairs of opposites rather than a simple list?
reflect.practice: Do one thing today for someone of a generation other than your own.

references.text: No comment of Sāyaṇa’s or Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara’s on this anuvāka is in the edition’s sources: Sāyaṇa’s anuvākas 52–57 are missing from the digital text used here, and neither commentary file glosses these words; the edition’s concordance maps give no anuvāka of theirs for it. The anonymous bhāṣya is the only commentary quoted.
The verse is also the tenth anuvāka of the Śrī Rudram (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.5.10), in this library’s Śrī Rudram edition.

flags.note: The Tirupati e-text lacks रीरिषः at the end of this anuvāka and has विधेम (the last word of 10.51) at its start: a matter of where that e-text draws the boundary, not a different reading. The Ānandāśrama text’s बधीः for वधीः is a misprint (corrections.json).
